steelman: The open-weight headline fuses two things that used to travel together: model access and data control. With a proprietary frontier model you always shipped your code to someone else's API, so 'MIT-licensed weights at one-sixth the cost' reads like the moment control finally comes back to you. GLM-5.2 makes the benchmark half of that real: it trails Opus 4.8 by a single point on FrontierSWE (74.4% vs 75.1%) and edges GPT-5.5 (72.6%) on long-horizon coding [s2], at roughly a sixth of the per-token price, and the vendor frames it as state-of-the-art long-horizon coding among open models [s1]. The defensible claim is conditional, not triumphalist: the license returns control only to the team that can actually run the weights, and at 753B parameters / 1.51TB [s3] almost nobody self-hosts. So the practical deployment is a hosted endpoint, and the MIT license that governs the weights does not govern your data flow: you inherit the operator's data governance exactly as you would with a closed model. The thesis is not 'open weights beat proprietary'; it is 'open weights decouple access from control, and the cost win survives only once you price the whole system, including where the model physically runs.'
strongest_attack: The 'you don't control your data anyway' claim is overstated, and the cost comparison cherry-picks the per-token rate. First, the 1.51TB barrier [s3] is a property of running it yourself, not of the license: open weights spawn a third-party host market, so you can pick an inference vendor in your jurisdiction or take a VPC / on-prem deployment that contracts for data residency in ways a closed API legally cannot offer. 'The open license stops protecting your data flow' is therefore false; open weights change the procurement surface even when you rent the compute. Second, 'one-sixth the cost' is a per-token figure, and long-horizon coding is the workload that burns the most tokens (more turns, larger contexts, more retries). The 1% FrontierSWE deficit [s2] compounds over long horizons into materially more failed-and-retried trajectories, so the per-completed-task gap narrows or inverts. The attack: the thesis treats 'can't self-host' as 'can't control your data' and quietly leans on a per-token headline the long-horizon workload undermines, so both load-bearing halves are weaker than stated.
reconciliation: The attack sharpens the thesis rather than refuting it, because it supplies the very nuance the thesis foregrounds. The thesis never claimed open weights are worthless or that residency is impossible; it claimed the headline 'MIT at one-sixth cost = default switch' is wrong because control and access decouple. The attack's own escape hatch (buy residency from a third-party host or a VPC deployment) is exactly the 'where you run it' tax the thesis names: it is procurement work and money, not a free property of the license. So the strengthened position is that the MIT license is necessary but not sufficient for data control; it converts a hard 'no' (a closed API you cannot contract around) into a 'yes, if you pay for self-hosting or a contracted residency host.' On cost, concede the token-accounting point outright: demote 'one-sixth' to a per-token figure and price long-horizon work per completed task, including the retry overhead implied by the 1% deficit [s2]. The thesis survives in the form it always intended: price the whole system (deployment path plus retries), not the per-token rate.
strengthened_argument: GLM-5.2's MIT license and near-frontier coding scores (74.4% vs Opus 4.8's 75.1%, ahead of GPT-5.5's 72.6% [s2]) are real, but they decouple two things the open-weight headline fuses: model access and data control. At 753B parameters / 1.51TB [s3] almost no team self-hosts, so the license's data-control payoff is realized only by paying for it, either with self-hosting hardware or a residency-bound third-party / VPC host. That is the 'where you run it' tax. The honest decision rule: GLM-5.2 wins when you can self-host or reach a compliant hosted endpoint AND your task's whole-system cost (per-completed-task tokens including retries from the roughly 1% benchmark deficit [s2], plus the deployment) beats a proprietary frontier model; a closed frontier model can be the cheaper whole-system call when data-residency forces an expensive deployment of weights you cannot run on commodity hardware. The license changes the procurement surface; it does not by itself change your data flow.
reason: The thesis is a falsifiable conditional that carves a real, non-obvious boundary (open weights decouple access from control; whole-system pricing dominates the per-token headline). The strongest attack (open weights still shift the procurement surface, and the per-token figure understates long-horizon cost) forces a genuine calibration but confirms the core mechanism rather than refuting it, so the thesis survives in strengthened form.
